title: One vice or two? Early exegetes already split

points.label: One vice, two words
points.text: **Ibn ʿAbbās** glosses the pair together: one who **reviles and disgraces** others. On this view the rhyming twin words name a single habit, doubled for force.
points.who: Ibn ʿAbbās, cited by Ibn Kathir

points.label: Gesture versus tongue
points.text: **Mujāhid** splits them by means: humaza wounds **with hand and eye**, lumaza **with the tongue**. Ibn Kathir links humaza to Q 68:11, the **hammāz** “going about with slander”.

points.label: Absent or face to face
points.text: Others split them by presence: hamz is **backbiting** in the victim’s absence, lamz **deriding** to the face. Some commentators give the **reverse**, so this line is not fixed either.
points.who: Maʿārif al-Qurʾān; Makarem Shirazi, Tafsir-e Nemuneh

bottom_text: No consensus. The early splits contradict each other, which leans toward one vice named twice; still open is whether the pair deliberately covers every way of wounding someone.
source_label: Ibn Kathir, Tafsir on Surah 104 · Maʿārif al-Qurʾān
